♻ ☆ ProSG: Learning Progressive Structural Guidance for 3D Human Pose Estimation
Zehua Wang, Qiongjie Cui, Changwang Mei, Huaijiang Sun, Pengqi Hu
For 3D human pose estimation from detected 2D joint locations, depth ambiguity remains a fundamental challenge. Even when two connected joints are accurately localized in the image, their relative depth along the camera axis can remain uncertain. Existing methods progressively refine pose representations through successive stages, with early stages emphasizing local 2D skeletal geometry and joint relationships and deeper stages developing increasingly depth-related representations. However, early-stage structural cues remain overlooked despite their importance for subsequent 3D inference. Our findings reveal that reusing such information provides complementary geometric guidance, particularly improving joint position estimation along the camera-space depth axis. We propose ProSG, a progressive structural guidance framework that preserves and aggregates intermediate pose representations from preceding stages to guide subsequent 3D pose refinement. Specifically, Structure Guided Accumulation (SGA) maintains a pool of these representations and adaptively retrieves relevant information for each joint and frame, enabling deeper stages to revisit early structural cues. Structural Context Reorganization (SCR) further reorganizes intermediate representations before they enter the representation pool, using compact structural contextual tokens to facilitate the effective integration of structural information across stages. Extensive experiments on Human3.6M and MPI-INF-3DHP demonstrate the effectiveness of ProSG, achieving state-of-the-art performance.
comment: 15page
♻ ☆ Reinforcing Diffusion Models by Instantaneous Trajectory Distribution Matching
Yihong Luo
Forward diffusion reinforcement learning (RL)---enabling deterministic ODE sampling without trajectory backpropagation---has grown increasingly popular for efficiently aligning diffusion models. However, we reveal that existing methods essentially rely on signed reward-weighted regression (RWR), regressing the trainable policy velocity onto rollouts from a behavior distribution. Unbiased baseline subtraction implicitly assumes that the policy velocity equals the behavior marginal velocity---an idealized assumption violated under classifier-free guidance (CFG) rollouts, offline/off-policy updates, and imperfect online self-consistency. This behavior--policy mismatch breaks baseline invariance and injects baseline-induced gradient drift, destabilizing training. To resolve this issue, we propose Instantaneous Trajectory Distribution Matching (iTDM), taking the infinitesimal limit of Trajectory Distribution Matching toward a time-local reward-guided target via the posterior-score identity to yield a sample-level gradient anchored at the behavior velocity without learning an additional reward-tilted target score. Tracking this velocity with an online auxiliary denoiser guarantees exact baseline invariance at the auxiliary optimum, effectively suppressing baseline drift across both online and offline RL. Extensive experiments across compositional generation, text rendering, and preference alignment show that iTDM achieves state-of-the-art in-domain and out-of-domain performance across group-wise online/offline RL and pairwise offline RL. Notably, on the challenging GenEval2 benchmark, iTDM converges nearly 3\times faster than competing methods while scaling smoothly to 0.87 without collapse. Furthermore, iTDM scales effectively to the 5.6B FLUX.3 model, achieving better performance across both in-domain and unseen metrics. Code is available at https://github.com/Luo-Yihong/iTDM

♻ ☆ SignSeek: Learning Transferable Representations for Sign Dictionary Retrieval WACV 2027
Sobhan Asasi, Ozge Mercanoglu Sincan, Richard Bowden
Sign language dictionaries are essential resources for sign language learners, yet automatically retrieving a sign from a dictionary, given only a query video, remains a challenging problem due to the natural variability between signers. Existing sign representation learning methods are built for closed-set recognition, producing embeddings that do not generalise to the open-set, signer-independent setting that retrieval demands. \textbf{SignSeek} closes this gap by contrastively learning sign representations with saliency-guided articulator masking. A contrastive objective aligns same-gloss signs across signers, while our Articulator Saliency-Guided Masking (ASGM) pinpoints the single most critical articulator per sign. This drives two complementary objectives, a masked contrastive alignment (MAC) loss that sees the sign through a single articulator and a masked prediction (MAP) loss that reconstructs it in latent space from the surrounding spatio-temporal context. Pretrained on 266K samples ($\sim$5,700 glosses) across multiple sign languages, \textbf{SignSeek} sets a new state-of-the-art performance in cross-corpus retrieval on ASL-Citizen, WLASL, and NMFs-CSL without any downstream fine-tuning. Strikingly, it achieves zero-shot generalisation to an entirely unseen British Sign Language (BSL), surpassing methods explicitly trained on BSL, and transfers seamlessly to isolated sign recognition and subtitle alignment, outperforming prior skeleton-based methods.

♻ ☆ Seeking the Unfamiliar but Memorable: Conceptual Creativity as Meta-Learning
Mengye Ren
What does it mean to create a new concept, rather than retrieve a familiar one? Repeatedly sampling a generative model at the same prompt produces variations with similar styles and typical content. We propose that creativity is the production of stimuli that are unfamiliar to an adaptive observer at first sight, but quickly learnable from a few exposures. We formalize this as a Creator-Appraiser pair: a Creator generates a candidate, an Appraiser adapts to it for a few inner-loop learning steps, and the Appraiser's improvement becomes the reward the Creator optimizes through. We instantiate the framework with diffusion as the Creator, an autoencoder Appraiser on MNIST, and a CLIP Appraiser with a low-rank adapter for natural images. With a frozen diffusion model and no additional language conditioning, the meta-learning gradient is enough to produce both stylistic variations and concept compositions beyond what the base model can generate on its own.

♻ ☆ Find the Fungible: Variable-Resolution Tokenization that Compacts Semantics with a Granularity Dial as a VLM "Catalyst"
Tianhao Fu, Austin Wang, Charles Chen, Roby Aldave-Garza, Victor Xie
Efficient vision-language models should preserve a useful representation of the whole image, even under tight budgets. However, aggressive pruning or indiscriminate merging can erase critical details and disrupt the spatial structure. We thus propose Varest, which maximizes semantic fungibility: tokens describing coherent content can be summarized together with minimal information loss. Object boundaries distilled from a visual foundation model guide grouping, while text localization protects details needed for reading. At lower budgets, Varest merges the image into coarser semantic regions, while maintaining full spatial coverage. After early language decoder layers process this representation, a learned selector prunes visual tokens that later layers no longer need, reducing repeated access to already integrated information. Across three LLaVA backbones and 13 benchmarks, Varest outperforms 10 training-free and 5 trained baselines in mean performance retention at every evaluated budget, preserving 86.10-92.33% of uncompressed performance using only 5.56% of tokens. This SOTA performance further generalizes to modern VLMs like Qwen3.8-27B.

♻ ☆ Learning to Generate in the Right Order
Julius Erbach, Dominik Narnhofer, Bernt Schiele, Jan Eric Lenssen, Konrad Schindler
We introduce PONDER, a method that learns in which order an image generator should fill in content and which of its earlier predictions to revise. Masked generative models construct a sample by repeatedly filling in subsets of missing variables. The order of these partial predictions determines the context available in subsequent steps and therefore affects the quality of the final sample. Common strategies are to choose the order randomly or based on local confidence estimates. Conditioned on the partially generated sample and the generator's features, our policy chooses which positions to fill next and/or which previously filled positions to mask for later regeneration, a mechanism we call rethinking. In this way, the generation process is able to adapt to the evolving context and also to revise earlier predictions. We optimize the policy using group-relative policy gradients, with rewards that measure constraint satisfaction, human preference, or distribution quality. For the latter, we introduce FIDgrad, an image-level reward derived from the (first-order) change in Fréchet Inception Distance caused by adding a generated sample to the current feature distribution. With the generators frozen, learned ordering reduces MAR-B ImageNet FID from 4.09 to 2.78, improves MaskGen-KL-XL HPSv2 from 24.50 to 26.50, and raises the accuracy on hard visual Sudokus from 4.5% to 56.6%, surpassing uncertainty-based greedy ordering (41.0%). Rethinking further improves these results to 2.70 FID, 27.80 HPSv2 and 96.7% accuracy.

♻ ☆ Self-Supervised Uncalibrated Multi-View Video Anonymization in the Operating Room
Keqi Chen, Vinkle Srivastav, Armine Vardazaryan, Cindy Rolland, Didier Mutter, Nicolas Padoy
Privacy preservation is a prerequisite for using video data in Operating Room (OR) research. Effective anonymization relies on the exhaustive localization of every individual; even a single missed detection necessitates extensive manual correction. However, existing approaches face two critical scalability bottlenecks: (1) they usually require manual annotations of each new clinical site for high accuracy; (2) while multi-camera setups have been widely adopted to address single-view ambiguity, camera calibration is typically required whenever cameras are repositioned. To address these problems, we propose a self-supervised multi-view video anonymization framework consisting of whole-body person detection and whole-body pose estimation, without annotation or camera calibration. Our core strategy is to enhance the single-view detector by "retrieving" false negatives using temporal and multi-view context, and conducting self-supervised domain adaptation. We first run an off-the-shelf whole-body person detector in each view with a low-score threshold to gather candidate detections. Then, we retrieve the low-score false negatives that exhibit consistency with the high-score detections via tracking and self-supervised uncalibrated multi-view association. These recovered detections serve as pseudo labels to iteratively fine-tune the whole-body detector. Finally, we apply whole-body pose estimation on each detected person, and fine-tune the pose model using its own high-score predictions. Experiments on the 4D-OR dataset of simulated surgeries and our dataset of real surgeries show the effectiveness of our approach achieving 99% and 97% recall, respectively. Moreover, we train a real-time whole-body detector using our pseudo labels, achieving comparable performance and highlighting our method's practical applicability. The code is available at https://github.com/CAMMA-public/OR_anonymization.
♻ ☆ AeroLLE: Nighttime Aerial Image Enhancement with Generated Supervision
Wei Lu, Hongyuan Liu, Liuqian Wang, Qi Ming, Xue Yang, Si-Bao Chen
Nighttime aerial image enhancement is constrained by the scarcity of aligned normal-light targets. Acquiring such targets from moving UAVs is difficult, and simple darkening of daytime images underrepresents the sensor noise, localized lighting, and uneven exposure of real nighttime captures. Generating normal-light references from real nighttime observations offers a practical way to fill this supervision gap. AeroNight pairs 1,200 real nighttime aerial RGB images with generated references selected through manual screening, preserving real imaging degradation in the inputs. This setting motivates AeroLLE, a lightweight two-stage framework whose context-aware Base Enhancer combines local processing with scene-level frequency information to recover visibility. Spatially Adaptive Exposure-Color Calibration (SAECC) then refines the base prediction through bounded low-resolution RGB gain and bias fields. AeroLLE achieves the highest PSNR and SSIM among the evaluated methods on both held-out test sets, reaching 17.62/17.89 dB PSNR and 0.5190/0.4964 SSIM on Test 1/Test 2, respectively. The model uses 255.24K parameters and 2.47G FLOPs, reducing FLOPs by 85.4\% relative to Multinex and improving PSNR by 1.56 dB on Test 2. AeroNight provides the first benchmark for pseudo-supervised nighttime aerial enhancement, and AeroLLE shows that generated references can support compact enhancement models.
♻ ☆ Off-Policy RL with Online Inference Tuning: 1st Place Solution to the CoRL 2026 RoboEval Challenge
Ilia Larchenko
The CoRL 2026 RoboEval challenge has eight bimanual tasks, and it ranks a policy not only on whether it succeeds but on how: every stage of the task, done safely, efficiently and with both arms in coordination, scored against human demonstrations. My solution has two parts. The generic part, carried over from my LeHome challenge solution, is off-policy RL on a $π_{0.5}$-based policy that is also its own value function. It is trained with AWR and RECAP on advantages of the exact official score, in a loop where every rollout is at the same time a Thompson-sampling trial of about 20 inference parameters. Out of the box, it took the policy to 0.85 RDS on held-out seeds in two days (and it was still very far from convergence). The competition-specific part adds data that local exploration cannot find: generated demonstrations that reach the full reward, and recovery episodes that start from the policy's own failures. The submitted policy reaches 0.990 RDS on my held-out seeds and 0.987 on the official seeds, and it won first place in the challenge, with 0.988 in the organisers' final evaluation on 1,000 unpublished seeds per task.

♻ ☆ Beyond Primitive Bloat: High-Fidelity Gaussian Splatting via Coordinate-Convolution Neural Network
Abhinav Kumar, Tristan Aumentado-Armstrong, Lazar Valkov, Gopal Sharma, Alex Levinshtein, Radek Grzeszczuk, Suren Kumar
Gaussian Splatting (GS) has revolutionized Novel View Synthesis (NVS) with fast training and real-time rendering, yet pushing its fidelity to arbitrary high levels remains an open challenge. We theoretically explain this barrier by proving that discrete Gaussian representations require an exponentially increasing number of primitives to raise training PSNR, which inevitably triggers optimization issues and validation overfitting. To bypass this scaling limit without primitive bloat, we formulate detail recovery as a continuous neural field over coarse renderings and prove that monotonically reducing approximation risk to zero requires jointly leveraging low-fidelity signals, local neighborhood, and coordinate queries. Guided by this result, we augment splatted renderings with an existing Coordinate-Convolution Neural Network (CCNN) that jointly convolves rendered low-fidelity signals with 2D pixel coordinate queries to synthesize residuals. Integrating CCNN into five diverse Gaussian Splatting baselines establishes new state-of-the-art fidelity across NVS benchmarks while preserving real-time rendering speeds with minimal training and storage overhead. Beyond NVS, they also consistently boost performance of 1D/2D regression and 2D super-resolution tasks.

♻ ☆ Editable Video Context: Mid-Context KV-Cache Reuse for Context-Managing Video LLMs
Dayu Wang, Shasha Xu
Context Language Models let a model edit its own context, while Suffix Cache Reuse makes edits to text efficient by adjusting the positions of cached keys for surviving tokens. We extend these ideas to video language models with multimodal rotary position embeddings (M-RoPE). We represent a long video as timestamped segments. After viewing a sparsely sampled version, the model selects segments for decoding at 4x the frame rate, and the remaining segments are removed from its context. Our rebuild method reuses the KV cache of surviving segments by rotating their keys with a single offset shared by the temporal, height, and width components of Qwen2.5-VL's M-RoPE. A content-hashed cache also avoids repeating vision-encoder computation for those segments. In preliminary experiments with Qwen2.5-VL-7B on synthetic needle-in-a-video-haystack questions over public-domain films, the method reduces prefill tokens and end-to-end rebuild latency relative to full recomputation while usually producing the same answer. Densifying the segment containing the answer improves accuracy when that segment is known. When the model selects segments itself, accuracy does not improve: it rarely identifies a needle that was absent from the sparse sample. We release the code, raw logs, and scripts used to reproduce the paper's results.
♻ ☆ ReCoCo: From Patches to Compositions for Visual Representation Learning
Juan Gutiérrez, Saman Zadtootaghaj, José Luis Blanco-Murillo, Sara Atito
Self-supervised learning has produced powerful visual representations, yet learning strong dense features remains challenging. While consistency between augmented views provides strong image-level supervision, extending this principle to local visual content is less straightforward. Existing approaches often match individual patches across views or identify coherent regions, introducing uncertainties in correspondence estimation and assumptions about how visual content should be grouped. We introduce ReCoCo (Regional Composition Consistency), a principled approach that extends cross-view consistency to the regional level without requiring such correspondences or semantic grouping. ReCoCo represents the content shared between augmented views through compositions of their patch-level predictions over learned visual prototypes. By aligning these compositions, the model learns from regions containing multiple visual concepts without requiring them to be separated beforehand. ReCoCo integrates naturally with teacher-student self-distillation and introduces no additional learned parameters. Extensive experiments demonstrate substantial improvements in frozen-feature segmentation, clustering, and regional retrieval while maintaining competitive image-level recognition, alleviating the trade-off between dense and global representation quality.
♻ ☆ AIR: Rethinking Image-Text Offset Alignment in Multimodal Contrastive Representation Space NeurIPS 2026
Guimeng Liu, Milad Abdollahzadeh, Ngai-Man Cheung
Image-text offset alignment, which refers to the consistency between visual transformation directions and their corresponding textual transformation directions, has become an important relational property in multimodal contrastive representation spaces such as CLIP and SigLIP. This property plays a central role in text-driven visual transformation tasks, including generative model domain adaptation and text-guided object-centric image editing, where textual offsets are used to guide visual transformations. These methods fundamentally rely on the assumption that image and text offsets are well aligned, such that textual transformation directions can provide reliable guidance for corresponding visual transformations. However, the validity of this alignment assumption has not been systematically examined. In this work, we question this foundational assumption by conducting a comprehensive empirical analysis of image-text offset alignment in multimodal contrastive representation space. Our findings reveal not only noticeable offset misalignment but also a meaningful positive correlation between image-text offset misalignment and semantic concept distance across six large datasets and eight contrastive vision-language models. Based on this discovery, we propose Adaptation with Iterative Refinement (AIR), a method that iteratively refines text offsets through anchor sampling and our proposed concept description learning to mitigate the downstream effect of image-text offset misalignment and improve guidance accuracy. Comprehensive experiments on zero-shot generative model domain adaptation and text-guided object-centric image editing across 40 setups, including qualitative, quantitative, and user studies, consistently show that AIR enables state-of-the-art performance in these tasks.
comment: Accepted to NeurIPS 2026
♻ ☆ ZIP: Scalable Crowd Counting via Zero-Inflated Poisson Modeling
Yiming Ma, Victor Sanchez, Tanaya Guha
The majority of crowd counting methods directly regress blockwise density maps using losses based on Mean Squared Error (MSE). This practice has two critical limitations: 1) it fails to account for the extreme spatial sparsity of annotations (i.e., over 95% of standard $8\times8$ blocks are empty across most benchmarks), which makes supervision signals in informative regions diluted by the predominant zeros. 2) MSE corresponds to a Gaussian error model that poorly matches discrete, non-negative count data. We introduce a novel crowd counting framework that is scalable and directly addresses the above limitations. This framework, named ZIP, models blockwise counts with a Zero-Inflated Poisson likelihood: A zero-inflation term models excess zeros in sparse annotations, while the Poisson component captures expected counts while respecting their discrete, non-negative nature. We provide a generalization analysis showing that the ZIP negative log-likelihood (NLL) has the same order of uniform generalization gap as Poisson NLL while offering a richer zero-inflated likelihood family, and that its bound scales more favorably with the number of spatial blocks than optimal-transport-based supervision. To assess the scalability and broad applicability of ZIP, we apply the same formulation across diverse backbones, from lightweight models to high-capacity architectures, spanning more than $100\times$ in both parameter count and inference FLOPs. Experiments on four standard crowd-counting benchmarks show that ZIP achieves state-of-the-art or highly competitive performance across a wide range of backbone capacities. Although ZIP is designed for sparse blockwise count maps, it also remains effective in dense crowd scenes, reducing MAE and RMSE by 3.9% and 8.5%, respectively, over mPrompt on UCF-QNRF. Code and trained weights are available at https://github.com/Yiming-M/ZIP.

♻ ☆ SIEVES: Selective Prediction Generalizes through Visual Evidence Scoring NeurIPS 2026
Hector G. Rodriguez, Marcus Rohrbach
As the accuracy of Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) on traditional visual question answering benchmarks approaches saturation, reliable deployment requires satisfying low error tolerances in real-world out-of-distribution (OOD) scenarios. Selective prediction aims to improve coverage, i.e. the share of inputs the system answers, while adhering to a user-defined risk level. This is typically achieved by assigning a confidence score to each answer and abstaining on those that fall below a certain threshold. Existing selective prediction methods rely on text-only reasoning and learn to predict confidences simply based on whether the answer was correct or not. In contrast, we introduce SIEVES (Selective Prediction through Visual Evidence Scoring), which first requires the answering model to provide visual evidence supporting its answer, by returning crops of the image alongside their textual reasoning and answer. Second, a lightweight selector is trained to predict the quality of this evidence, assessing how well the provided crops localize the relevant visual elements and if the final answer is coherent with this evidence. We show that SIEVES improves coverage by up to six times on challenging OOD benchmarks (V* Bench, HR-Bench-8k, MME-RealWorld-Lite, VizWiz, and AdVQA), compared to non-grounding baselines. Beyond better generalization to OOD tasks, the design of the SIEVES selector enables transfer to proprietary reasoners without access to their weights or logits, such as o3 and Gemini-3-Pro, providing coverage boosts beyond those attributable to accuracy alone. We highlight that SIEVES generalizes across all tested OOD datasets and reasoner models, without benchmark- or reasoner-specific training or adaptation.
comment: 45 pages. NeurIPS 2026 camera-ready version. Code: https://github.com/hector-gr/SIEVES
♻ ☆ BARISTA: A Multi-Task Egocentric Benchmark for Compositional Visual Understanding ICML 2026
Patrick Knab, Orgest Xhelili, Inis Buzi, Drago Andres Guggiana Nilo, Mohd Saquib Khan, Lorenz Kolb, Manuel Scherzer, Kerem Yildirir, Christian Bartelt, Philipp Johannes Schubert
Scene understanding is central to general physical intelligence, and video is a primary modality for capturing both state and temporal dynamics of a scene. Yet understanding physical processes remains difficult, as models must combine object localization, hand-object interactions, relational parsing, temporal reasoning, and step-level procedural inference. Existing benchmarks usually evaluate these capabilities separately, limiting diagnosis of why models fail on procedural tasks. We introduce BARISTA, a densely annotated egocentric dataset and benchmark of 185 real-world coffee-preparation videos covering fully automatic, portafilter-based, and capsule-based workflows. BARISTA provides verified per-frame scene graphs linking persistent object identities to masks, tracks, boxes, attributes, typed relations, hand-object interactions, activities, and process steps. From these graphs, we derive zero-shot language-based tasks spanning phrase grounding, hand-object interaction recognition, referring, activity recognition, relation extraction, and temporal visual question answering. Experiments reveal strong variation across task families and no consistently dominant model family, positioning BARISTA as a challenging diagnostic benchmark for procedural video understanding. Code and dataset available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/ramblr/BARISTA.
comment: Accepted CTB Workshop at ICML 2026
♻ ☆ Sparse-View Interpretable 3D Animal Behavior Representations for Neural Encoding and Decoding
Xinming Dai, Qihang Jin, Jiaying Zhang, Tianshu Tan, Baiyuan Chen, Hanrui Lyu, Lenny Aharon, Kyle Daruwalla, Xun Helen Hou, Matthew R. Whiteway, Liam Paninski, Yizi Zhang
A deeper understanding of brain function requires a precise, structured characterization of behavior. Yet, extracting behavioral representations from video in a form suitable for scientific analysis remains a fundamental challenge. Many prior studies represent behavior via pose estimation or nonlinear video embeddings. However, pose tracking discards rich information beyond predefined keypoints, while nonlinear video embeddings lack interpretability. We address this limitation with SABLE (Sparse-view Animal Behavior Latent Embeddings), a self-supervised framework that leverages a geometric inductive bias to learn behavior representations. By augmenting a multi-view transformer with priors from monocular depth and pose estimation, SABLE reconstructs 3D animal behavior from extremely sparse views while learning explicit 3D latent structure. Without ground-truth 3D labels, it reliably recovers 3D behavior from two-view videos, whereas state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods fail or yield degenerate solutions. Across the International Brain Lab and Cheese3D datasets, we demonstrate that SABLE learns 3D representations that match or exceed prior SOTA performance in neural encoding and decoding. Single-neuron analyses further identify neurons with putative 3D tuning, generating testable hypotheses about how the brain represents 3D behavior. Once pretrained across animals, SABLE serves as an off-the-shelf model that generalizes zero-shot to unseen animals without animal-specific calibration or retraining. Our method establishes 3D-aware video embeddings that capture complex behavior, opening new avenues for studying brain-behavior relationships.
comment: Add Jiaying Zhang to the author list
♻ ☆ dKV Forcing: Separating Generation and Memory Representations through a Differentiable KV Cache
Zhiqi Li, Bo Zhu
A causal video generator writes every segment it produces into a key--value (KV) cache, and later segments know the past only through it. Self-rollout training stops the gradient at this cache, and Self Gradient Forcing (SGF) restores it, but applies it to the same weights that generate the current segment. We find that writing and generating are different roles: in a pretrained generator the written KV already differs from the KV used for denoising, and on shared weights the gradient from future reads is negatively aligned with the gradient of generation. We propose dKV Forcing (dKV denotes differentiable KV), which gives the write its own parameters, a low-rank residual used only when a segment enters the cache, and trains them with the gradient of the later segments that read what they wrote. Opening this gradient through the cache in common use exhausts GPU memory. We trace this to checkpoint replay re-writing the cache, not to the gradient path, which removes the need for the second reconstruction pass of SGF. dKV Forcing keeps the cache as persistent differentiable pages and computes the exact gradient in one temporal traversal, with an $11\%$ lower memory peak and $28\%$ less resident memory. With pages that store hidden states, it trains 15\,s clips on which the two-pass reconstruction runs out of memory. Trained on 5\,s clips, dKV Forcing reaches the highest VBench-Long quality score at 60\,s and 240\,s and outperforms SGF by $3.6$ and $6.1$ points of aesthetic quality, with a higher dynamic degree.
♻ ☆ RS-JEPA: Remote Sensing Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture with Scan-Path Views for Cross-Sensor Image Retrieval
Tanishq Rachamalla, Srishti Kaushik, Muhammad Attique Khan, Swalpa Kumar Roy
Cross-sensor remote sensing image retrieval aims to find scenes with the same content across heterogeneous sensors, such as SAR and optical or panchromatic (PAN) and multispectral (MS) imagery, without manual labels. Existing self-supervised methods either reconstruct sensor-specific pixel detail, align each image only with its co-registered twin, or rely on large transformers with 118-173M parameters (and up to 398M). We introduce RS-JEPA, a compact joint-embedding predictive framework built on a Vision Mamba encoder shared by both sensors. Since a state-space encoder reads an image as an ordered sequence of patches, we propose scan-path views, which treat two reading orders of the same image as two views with identical pixels and predict the hidden patches in one order from the visible patches in the other.To keep this prediction challenging, we propose Adversarial View Coupling (AVC), which learns the hardest split of the visible patches, and a neighbourhood consensus loss that aligns the scene similarities of both sensors. Extensive experiments on SAR-optical (BEN-14K, CBRSIR-VS) and PAN-MS (DSRSID) benchmarks demonstrate that RS-JEPA achieves the highest F1@5 among twelve re-implemented methods (72.92, 80.35 and 94.43) with a retrieval network of only 3.88M parameters (14.57M in training, 8-16times fewer than prior JEPA retrievers). Like prior methods, RS-JEPA trains on co-registered pairs. Our results highlight reading order as a source of self-supervised views. code: https://github.com/Tanishq251/RSJEPA.
Information Retrieval
☆ SAG-Mem-1.0 Technical Report
Yuchao Wu, XingCheng Liang, Xuanze Wang, Yini Huang, Yue Wu
Long-term conversational memory requires retrieving complementary facts scattered across dialogue sessions, including intermediate evidence with limited similarity to the original question. Existing approaches often rely on derived memory representations or persistent relational structures, introducing construction costs and potentially losing source details. We present SAG-Mem, a conversational memory framework that preserves complete dialogue messages in non-overlapping chunks and discovers complementary evidence through query-time lexical expansion. Memory construction requires no model inference, using a lexical index without LLM-based extraction, summarization, or semantic relation construction. At query time, BM25 retrieves initial candidates, an evidence evaluator identifies useful chunks, and lexical cues from selected evidence guide an additional retrieval round. Retrieved dialogue is further annotated with calendar interpretations of supported relative-time expressions, preserving the original wording and temporal granularity. We also introduce SAG-Mem-Lite, an alternative configuration that replaces evidence scoring with embedding-based candidate scoring, achieving lower operational cost than Full Context and all memory-based baselines across both benchmarks with low query latency. On LoCoMo and LongMemEval, SAG-Mem achieves overall scores of 83.08 and 80.20, respectively, the highest among the evaluated methods on both benchmarks. On LongMemEval, it exceeds the strongest compared baseline by 7.20 points. SAG-Mem-Lite achieves scores of 77.09 and 77.20, respectively. These results support dialogue preservation and evidence-guided retrieval expansion as an effective design for long-term conversational memory.
☆ Delegent: A Multi-Agent Harness That Reduces Cost without Sacrificing Performance
Lingwei Gu, Jimmy Lin
Agents built on frontier language models are expensive. At every step, the frontier model re-reads its entire context and executes every subtask regardless of its difficulty. This paper explores the simple thesis that much of this cost can be removed by delegating easy subtasks to a small language model, or SLM, that runs on hardware one already owns. To test it, we build Delegent, a simple and effective agent harness built on Claude Code, in which the frontier model stays in charge of every task but hands focused subtasks, such as investigating code, running tests, and searching a corpus, to SLM subagents. Existing approaches such as cascades and model routers usually choose which model executes the entire task, whereas in Delegent, the frontier model always leads the execution and delegates easy subtasks to the SLM. No router or model is trained, so either model can be swapped freely. With the help of a 27B FP8 SLM, Delegent reduces the frontier cost of long-horizon coding by 67% and of agentic search by 59%, with no loss in task performance, and even a 2B SLM that fits on a laptop reduces the coding cost by 66%. The savings grow with the legwork that the frontier model would otherwise do itself, and a short instruction, which leaves the main coding tasks to the frontier model, accounts for most of the saving and keeps the 2B SLM from losing tasks. Code: https://github.com/castorini/delegent

☆ Towards Realistic Evaluation of Uncertainty Quantification for LLM-Based Recommender Systems
Hao Wu, Sipeng Chen, Weikai Li, Tianyi Chen, Qiancheng Yang, Hang Zhou, Yizhou Sun, Wei Wang, Xiao Luo
Large language models (LLMs) provide a flexible interface for recommendation systems. However, their issued rankings require reliable instance-level uncertainty monitoring. In this scenario, comparing uncertainty quantification (UQ) methods becomes challenging because LLM rankers lack a standard item-classification head. Their scores may depend on option labels, prompts, generation procedures, and the available user and item evidence. Existing methods derive uncertainty from different sources and apply it at different stages of the recommendation process. Some methods evaluate an issued ranking, whereas others use uncertainty to change the ranking itself, making direct comparison difficult. Here we introduce a fixed-ranking benchmark which evaluates eight heterogeneous UQ signals as record-level monitors under a shared output contract. We evaluate these signals across four recommendation datasets and two LLM backbones under a shared fixed-ranking protocol. From the results, we draw three main observations. First, UQ method ordering changes across backbones even on the same reference instances. Second, ranking-aligned Top10Mass provides the strongest scalar Error@10 detection in several evaluation conditions, reflecting effective cutoff-aligned monitoring, while its advantage narrows for popularity-tail targets. Third, scalar UQ signals are weak at identifying which control has the larger clipped NDCG@10 difference, whereas source-specific signals, including Perturbation Rank Instability and simple listwise distances, provide stronger paired-control agreement, reflecting their sensitivity to the two controlled evidence sources. These findings motivate us to evaluate ranking-failure detection, robustness across recommendation conditions, and responses to controlled evidence changes as distinct properties of UQ.
comment: 27 pages, 5 figures. Published in Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR), 11/2026. Reviewed on OpenReview: https://openreview.net/forum?id=GXDe6REdu3
☆ SOARS: System One Assisted Reranking for Agentic Search
Amin Bigdeli, Liye Fu, Fattane Zarrinkalam, Joel Stremmel, Elizabeth Lingg
Deep search agents address complex information needs through iterative retrieval and reasoning, where the relevance of retrieved evidence influences downstream performance. Existing rerankers improve retrieval effectiveness but introduce substantial latency and cost when invoked throughout the search trajectory. We introduce SOARS, a training-free framework leveraging a System One model for fast, calibrated relevance estimation. At each search step, SOARS selects query-relevant passages from long documents and reranks candidates in a single call, jointly considering the original question and agent-generated sub-query. Across six LLM backbones on BrowseComp-Plus and WebShaper, SOARS consistently improves answer accuracy and evidence recall while reducing search calls, end-to-end latency, and inference cost. On BrowseComp-Plus, it improves GPT-5.4 Mini's accuracy from 73.9% to 84.7% while reducing search calls from 23 to 14, demonstrating the potential of System One reranking for more effective and efficient deep search.
☆ Speculative Decoding for Semantic-ID-Based Generative Recommendations
Harshal A. Chaudhari
Generative recommender systems with Semantic IDs (SIDs) represent each item as a short sequence of $L$ discrete tokens and use a sequence model to predict the next item's tokens from a user's history. Industry-scale deployments typically use these models to retrieve multiple candidates per request with constrained beam search. However, this incurs a fixed cost of $L$ sequential model calls per request, and accuracy degrades as the SID generator becomes less sharp, without a guarantee on how close the output is to the exact top-$K$. Production systems therefore cannot detect degraded retrieval for individual requests. We propose SIDECAR, which uses approximate draft candidates and a tree-attention pass to score the entire draft in a single model call, memory permitting. This pass bounds the probability of every unexplored SID prefix and certifies the exact top-$K$ if the draft contains them. Otherwise, a branch-and-bound fallback expands only the parts of the trie that can still change the output, reaching certification within at most $L$ calls for any draft. Moreover, under a budget of $M$ tokens per call and $Y$ calls, which for $Y = L$ matches the resources of a beam search of width $M$, SIDECAR announces a factor $1 + δ$ within which its list will be exact at every rank. Depending on model sharpness, SIDECAR returns the exact top-$K$ using a fraction of beam search's calls or memory. Even when the budget is too small to recover the exact top-$K$, SIDECAR, unlike beam search, reports the announced factor, allowing the serving system to stop early once a quality target or latency limit is reached.

☆ A Text-to-SQL Benchmark for Official Statistics
Lucas Lageweg, Karen Goes, Tom van den Broek, Frank Pijpers, Paul Groth, Jan-Christoph Kalo
Official statistics are critical datasets for a wide variety of actors, including policymakers and businesses. For providers of official statistics, improving accessibility, governance, and disclosure of their data is of key importance. This can be improved by providing question-answering systems based on text-to-SQL approaches. However, existing text-to-SQL benchmarks do not resemble this setting. Official statistics are published as open-domain catalogs of thousands of wide tables whose columns and values are codes, and whose meaning is recorded in separate metadata rather than in a relational schema. To address this gap, we introduce LOCuST, a text-to-SQL benchmark that pairs over two thousand English and Dutch tables from Statistics Netherlands with a semantic knowledge graph. The graph describes the tables, measures, and dimension codes through labels, definitions, hierarchies, and units, and is the external knowledge a system needs to find the right tables and ground a question in the right codes. The benchmark includes expert-annotated questions for different query and aggregation types, including raw value retrieval, summations, proportion calculations, and joins. Alongside standard evaluation measures, we introduce an observation F1 metric that measures how close a query is to the ground truth even when the answers are different. We evaluate a variety of state-of-the-art LLMs and find that they struggle to write SQL that answers the questions correctly.
☆ LazUnirec: Unifying Retrieval and Ranking in Multi-scenario Industrial Recommendation
Xiaodong Li, Junfeng Zhang, Shichao Nie, Ziyue Guo, Yiming Liu, Xinxin Xu, Xurong Li, Jinyuan Dang, Zhanming Ou, Jianan Yan, Tao Luo, Xiaoyi Zeng
Modern industrial recommendation systems typically divide retrieval and ranking into two separate cascaded stages, leading to inconsistent optimization objectives, redundant encoding of user sequences, and a waste of computational resources. Previous efforts have investigated using Transformers to model both retrieval and ranking simultaneously. However, these studies still face two major limitations: (1) Since retrieval and ranking share a single Transformer backbone, the gradient conflict arises when the gradient directions of the two tasks are inconsistent. (2) When gradient conflict occurs, the model cannot determine a reliable direction for gradient updates. To this end, we propose a Unified Retrieval and Ranking approach for Multi-scenario Industrial Recommendation, termed as LazUnirec. Specifically, we construct task-shared and task-private parameters on the Transformer backbone to mitigate the gradient conflict. Wherein, for the attention components, we propose LoRA-modulated attention, enabling retrieval and ranking to share attention parameters while preserving task-private parameters. For the feed-forward networks (FFN), we present task-adaptive sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) to mitigate gradient conflict by constructing task-shared and task-private experts. Moreover, we propose an uncertainty estimation that evaluates the gradient reliability of the retrieval and ranking, thereby guiding the model toward a more reliable gradient update direction when gradient conflict occurs. In addition, knowledge distillation from ranking to retrieval further enables cross-task knowledge transfer. Extensive offline experiments and online A/B testing demonstrate the effectiveness and superiority of LazUnirec. LazUnirec has been deployed in online multi-scenario industrial recommendation system and currently delivers significant gains for the platform.
☆ See the Answer, Learn to Embed: Learning Universal Multimodal Embeddings from Hindsight
Yoonki Cho, Youngju Na, Taegeun Yang, Jinhwan Seo, Sung-Eui Yoon
Universal Multimodal Embedding (UME) models map heterogeneous multimodal inputs into a shared embedding space, where pairwise similarity supports diverse downstream tasks. Recent reasoning-driven UME approaches use intermediate reasoning to generate additional context for embedding, but often incur extra computation at inference. In this paper, we explore the matched candidate (i.e., the paired target) as an alternative source of context, asking whether a model can "see the answer" during training and "learn to embed" without it at inference. However, direct conditioning on this privileged context can introduce candidate-specific information unavailable from the query alone or cause the candidate-conditioned query representation to collapse toward the candidate embedding. To address this, we introduce Hindsight-Enhanced Multimodal Embeddings (HEME), which learns query-grounded hindsight representations from such candidate context. HEME first trains a hindsight teacher with a hindsight attention mask, mismatched-candidate conditioning, and query-token alignment to limit excessive reliance on the candidate. It then freezes the teacher and distills its hindsight representation and similarity distribution into a standalone student embedder. At inference, the student independently encodes queries and candidates without candidate conditioning or the hindsight teacher. Experiments on MMEB-V2 and the agent and text tasks of MMEB-V3 demonstrate the effectiveness of HEME and show that it enables more efficient inference than explicit reasoning-driven methods.
☆ Unjamming Deferrals: Supporting Students Through JAMN Bot, a Mobile RAG-Grounded Policy Assistant
Mark Farinas, Alesandra Garcia, Maria Reyes, Jethro Nueva, Nawaf Qureshi, Mahmoud Elsaadany, Shokry Shamseldin
In some educational institutions, workflows such as the exam deferral process can be slow, inconvenient, and inconsistent, which creates the need to implement novel digital systems. This paper presents Schedulater, a mobile app for managing university exam deferrals. JAMN Bot is a Large Language Model (LLM)-powered chatbot integrated into Schedulater that provides context-aware support to help users understand the deferral process. The system features a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline using Ollama (Llama 3.2 3B) for self-hosted inference which enables policy-grounded responses without sacrificing privacy. We evaluate the system using a 43-item benchmark spanning Exam Deferral, Privacy, Scheduling, Cross-Policy, and Adversarial & Out-of-Scope questions, and report inter-rater agreement among our human evaluators alongside retrieval hit-rate metrics. Subsequently, we utilize an LLM-as-a-judge approach with GPT-5.4, revealing slight-to-moderate alignment with our raters that improves with answer quality, and check the ranking against a panel including Gemini 3.5 Flash and Qwen3.5 397B. The results of our study display trade-offs between open-weight and frontier models, as well as LLM-human evaluation alignment with answer quality. Schedulater demonstrates the feasibility of integrating lightweight LLMs into university administrative workflows with structured retrieval.

☆ OmniEVIE: Evidence-Vector-Informed Embedding for Multi-modal Retrieval
Zifei Wang, Wei Wen, Qiang Ji, Qian-Wen Zhang, Ruizhi Qiao, He Liu, Xing Sun, Qiang Lin
Multimodal retrieval must match dense pages, fine-grained entities, ordered video, and agent tools and memory. Single-vector embeddings lose local evidence, cross-encoders reread every recalled item online, and uncompressed late interaction is too large to serve. We present OmniEVIE, a 4.5B multi-vector embedding model covering text, images, visual documents, video, and tools with one compressed index and a three-stage retriever. Each record stores at most 128 int8 vectors of dimension 64 (9,472 bytes, or 8.82 GiB per million records), providing a mean vector, 1-bit signs, and int8 multi-vectors for coarse, middle, and final search while localizing each hit to a page region or video interval. Training, merging, indexing, and retrieval are co-designed: all tasks share one retrieval format, a three-grade evidence check removes false negatives, dynamic sampling follows the baseline-teacher gap, candidates are compressed with ST-HAC during training to match the index, stage-wise and specialist models are merged by parameter block, and a saliency gate with a noise floor refines query scoring. Trained on public datasets, OmniEVIE scores 60.68 (full d=2048 sequence) and 60.06 (K128 x d64 int8 index) on MMEB-V3 (190 tasks), 77.96 on MMEB-V2 (78 tasks), and 62.96 on ViDoRe V3 (48 tasks). On 1M and 5M records, a single-thread query takes 54.2 ms and 120.2 ms (11.1x and 25.3x faster than exact 4096-d single-vector search; 236x and 532x faster than full int8 MaxSim). Video is encoded directly from frames without a parsing model: on QVHighlights (1,083 queries), the peak falls inside the labeled segment for 78.0% of queries and the returned span (18% of video length) intersects it for 94.3% vs. 44.9% random. Weights and code: https://huggingface.co/tencent/OmniEVIE-4B and https://github.com/Tencent/OmniEVIE.

☆ LARF: Learning-aligned Reasoning Framework for Search Relevance WSDM 2027
Tian Tang, Guo Chen, Reed Li, Hao Wang, Yu Lu, Haijin Liang, Haibo Shi
Query-document relevance estimation is a core component of AI-native search systems, where a model must assess whether retrieved documents satisfy users' information needs under complex, multi-dimensional criteria. However, directly applying large language models (LLMs) to this task remains challenging because conventional supervised fine-tuning (SFT) provides limited supervision for domain-specific judgment rationales, while standard trajectory-level reinforcement learning (RL) objectives do not explicitly enforce margin separation among adjacent ordinal relevance labels. Moreover, although such reasoning can be useful during training, chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning is impractical for latency-sensitive online ranking. These challenges make it difficult to resolve ambiguous decision boundaries. We propose a three-stage framework LARF (Learning-Aligned Reasoning Framework for Search Relevance): it first performs cold-start SFT on strategically selected samples with multi-agent guided CoT rationales, then applies discriminative GRPO with attribute-wise, list-wise, and rule-consistency rewards together with a margin loss on the terminal relevance token, and finally distills the teacher into a dual-head student whose classification heads are retained for non-autoregressive inference. On a human-annotated web search relevance benchmark with approximately 300K training and 16K test instances, LARF-8B improves six-class classification accuracy by 5.78 percentage points and NDCG by 5.05 points, while the classification-only serving path reduces inference latency by 82.9\%. These results indicate that aligning structured reasoning, terminal decision optimization, and classification-head distillation can provide an effective accuracy--efficiency trade-off for industrial search relevance modeling.

☆ User-Adaptive Fusion of Multiple Foundation Models for Recommender Systems WSDM 2027
Sunwoo Kim, Hyunjin Hwang, Geon Lee, Kyungho Kim, Kijung Shin
Can recommender systems benefit from combining a collection of foundation models within and across modalities? While different foundation models may capture complementary aspects of item metadata, we find that naively combining their representations yields only marginal gains over using a single foundation model. We make a key observation: the users who benefit vary across foundation models. Motivated by this observation, we introduce UF2O, a user-adaptive approach for fusing multiple foundation models for recommendation. In a nutshell, UF2O models the contribution of each foundation model as user-specific by maintaining separate recommendation views and adaptively combining their scores for each user. By performing fusion at the score level, UF2O can also fuse heterogeneous foundation models without directly aligning their representation spaces. Extensive experiments that jointly combine four foundation models on four datasets show that UF2O outperforms existing fusion approaches in both static and sequential recommendation settings, with improvements of up to 7% over the strongest fusion baseline. The code, datasets, and supplementary materials for our work are available at https://github.com/kswoo97/UFFO.

☆ MELODI: Similarity-Identity Decoupling for Lightweight Ranking
Quoc Phong Nguyen, Vuong Le, Volodymyr Vaskovych, Julien Monteil
For latency-constrained candidate ranking, we propose a similarity-identity decoupling framework that separates target-history compatibility from target-only information. We study two orders for computing pooled similarity, similarity-then-pool and pool-then-similarity, and identify linearity of the similarity operator in its history argument, for each fixed target, as sufficient for their equivalence, justifying the cheaper pool-then-similarity form. We instantiate the framework as multi-head efficient lightweight operator for decoupling identity and similarity (MELODI), whose similarity branch combines target-conditioned multi-head history pooling with a single residual-free cross layer that is linear in its pooled-history input and whose identity branch is problem-dependent. On public benchmark datasets, MELODI matches or surpasses the evaluated target-aware and target-agnostic baselines. On two large-scale industrial datasets, its area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC), normalised discounted cumulative gain (NDCG), and recall values are equal to or higher than those of the evaluated target-aware baselines. Processor measurements show lower latency than the evaluated candidate-conditioned baselines at large candidate counts, further reduced by request-local history reuse.
☆ RELAY: Learning Compatible Representations One Encoder at a Time
Yu Wang, Chuan Qin, Qiang Zhang
Old and new document embeddings coexist during incremental gallery re-encoding. RELAY trains a new query encoder with a learned projection against the original gallery, then freezes both to train the new document encoder. The same query vector scores both document versions throughout a single re-encoding pass. After backfill, optional query refinement drops the projection and reuses the stored document vectors. Across three text-to-image retrieval upgrades on COCO and Flickr30K, RELAY improves Recall@1 on untouched galleries by 8.66-10.23 percentage points over the original systems. For direct re-encoding, RELAY ranks first in both Qwen-to-Qwen upgrades and second in CLIP-to-Qwen by area under the Recall@1 curve, under both native scoring and matched calibration. With embeddings held fixed, calibrating scores separately for each document version can reduce drops in Recall@1 during backfill and change which method achieves the highest backfill AUC. After query refinement, final Recall@1 is within 0.97 percentage points of conventional joint training in all three upgrades.

☆ Community Notes Across Platforms: Evaluating the Feasibility of Re-using Crowd-sourced Context Notes
Nishka Arora, Yann Issam Aouidef, Ashish Goel
Crowdsourced fact-checking systems such as Community Notes can provide useful context for misleading content. Producing and rating new notes on such systems requires substantial contributor effort. However, the resulting context is typically confined to the post and platform for which it was created. We ask whether already-vetted notes can be reused when the same claims recur across posts and platforms. To investigate this question, we construct a human-labelled dataset using Community Notes attached to X posts created during a one-week period and candidate posts retrieved from Bluesky. Within our observation window, 140 of 340 claims had at least one confirmed recurrence on Bluesky, showing that cross-platform note reuse is a substantial opportunity. Recurrence alone, however, does not establish whether reuse would provide timely context. A timing analysis shows that many relevant notes were already Helpful when matching Bluesky posts appeared. Even when a Bluesky post appeared first, reuse could often still provide context sooner after publication than the original X post received its Helpful note. To automate the discovery of these opportunities, we evaluate a three-stage pipeline that searches the Bluesky stream for potential recurrences and determines whether an existing note applies. The pipeline achieves 72.6% precision in a held-out stream evaluation and 70.1% end-to-end recall on our known-positive set. We further characterize the pipeline's costs and principal failure modes. Crossnote, our prototype Bluesky labeler, implements this approach by applying existing Community Notes to matching posts. Our findings suggest that reusing vetted crowdsourced context is a compelling way to scale the reach and impact of Community Notes. Note reuse can complement the production of new notes by reducing duplicated effort and shortening time to context when misleading claims recur.
☆ CA-RAG: Constraint-Aligned Retrieval for Structurally Faithful Long-Form Generation
Vimal Kumar Kumar, Meghana Kshirsagar, Conor Ryan
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) typically optimises evidence selection for semantic relevance, whereas compliance-sensitive long-form generation also requires evidence supporting explicit structural obligations. Semantically relevant retrieval may therefore omit information needed for mandatory downstream clauses. We propose Constraint-Aligned RAG (CA-RAG), a retrieval-conditioning framework that augments section-specific queries with ontology-derived structural constraints and policy-grounded knowledge-graph relations before evidence selection. Retrieval-only evaluation with manually annotated evidence shows consistent improvements across retrieval budgets. At $k=6$, CA-RAG increases Precision@$k$ from $0.5268$ to $0.5692$, pooled Recall@$k$ from $0.5402$ to $0.5950$, and F1@$k$ from $0.5389$ to $0.5672$ over standard RAG. Generation experiments further show improvements in compliance and reliability in several model--domain settings, while generation-only constraints achieve higher clause coverage but lower overall compliance and reliability. These results indicate that structurally aligned retrieval can improve evidence sufficiency in compliance-sensitive long-form generation.

On eight public datasets from five platforms, we compare four structural predictors, which use nothing about the learner beyond the last activity, with ten personalised recommenders and with open-weight LLM rankers from 0.5 to 7 billion parameters, under two protocols. The structural predictors reach between 0.81 and 1.00 of the best accuracy of any method (median 0.95), mostly through population transitions rather than the course order; the best personalised recommender is significantly better on five datasets, by 0.007 to 0.102 NDCG@10, and on Eedi in three of four training runs. Every method is far less accurate on steps along transitions never seen in training and on steps chosen by learners. LLM rankers look competent with random negatives but are never much better than a word-matching baseline, and with negatives that are plausible under the course structure they stay close to random or well behind the transition heuristic, whatever their size. In a simulation with known learner needs, the structural share tracks the share of steps decided by the platform, and offline accuracy ranks an oracle of the learners' needs below imitators of the platform. Weighting test steps by how unlikely the structure makes them restores much of the link with usefulness and, on the real data, reveals a significant personalisation signal on seven of the eight datasets. We propose a syllabus-aware evaluation checklist and release a Python package that reports the lift of any recommender over the structure.

♻ ☆ GEM: A Generative Embedding Model Bridging Reasoning and Retrieval EACL 2027

Modern LLMs excel at reasoning and instruction following, enabling users to express increasingly complex information needs. However, existing retrievers largely rely on matching surface-level relevance, creating a growing gap between the evolving nature of user queries and how the queries are interpreted by retrievers. In this paper, we present GEM, a generative embedding model that augments retrieval by leveraging its internal knowledge to reason about user intent and relevance criteria prior to embedding. GEM unifies generation and embedding in a sequential manner, where encoding can be conceptually viewed as processing only one additional token during autoregressive generation. Unlike conventional query expansion, GEM learns to produce embeddings aligned with its reasoning, moving beyond surface-level matching. Furthermore, the generative nature allows GEM to be prompted like standard instruction-tuned LLMs and enables test-time compute scaling for retrieval. Compared with a non-reasoning variant of the same backbone, GEM achieves approximately 35% relative improvement in nDCG@10 on BRIGHT, a benchmark of challenging queries requiring reasoning, and 70% in p-MRR on FollowIR, a benchmark evaluating retrievers' ability to understand and follow user instructions. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of activating an embedding model's internal reasoning capabilities to improve retrieval. Our code and model are publicly available at https://github.com/ZhlSh17/GEM and https://huggingface.co/gem-search/GEM-4B, respectively.

Using empirical retrieval frequencies across sampled reference queries as a relevance proxy, CACO formulates a label-free coverage objective that improves recall across all 30 backbone-dataset settings in offline experiments. To avoid the overhead of sampling reference queries at inference, CACO employs a coordinated query adjustment network combining inter-query bidirectional attention with gated relative directions, updating queries via bounded tangent-space projection and spherical retraction. During training, CACO applies tangential antithetic perturbations and counterfactual single-query replacement to measure each query's marginal gain, yielding an unbiased gradient estimator of smoothed set coverage across non-differentiable ANN search. On eight public benchmarks and an in-house 24-partition streaming industrial dataset, CACO improves Recall@100 and Recall@400 by up to 23.7% and 23.9% over the strongest baseline, cuts inter-query overlap by 53.3%-64.9%, and adds only 0.5%-3.0% inference latency.

We show that no method we tested on the frozen token embeddings recovers this constraint; the difficulty lies in identifying the excluded topic, which depends on the query alone. EXCISE therefore confines learning to the query path and leaves the index frozen. Two query-side modules (1.5M parameters in total) detect the excluded topic and re-embed a 100-document shortlist, and a parameter-free rule demotes the candidates that match it. It raises ExcluIR success@10 from 0.10-0.22 to 0.84-0.85 and Boolean NOT accuracy from 0.25-0.29 to 0.84-0.92. Pooled over 1,860 test queries, EXCISE matches the strongest fine-tuned cross-encoder (568M parameters) while preserving the retrieval quality of its frozen index, whereas fine-tuned rerankers degrade ordinary retrieval. To support further work, we release X-BENCH, a tiered benchmark of explicit, cue-free and compound exclusions with no-harm and Boolean controls.

Multimodal embedding models aim to map heterogeneous inputs, such as text, images, videos, and audio, into a shared semantic space. However, existing methods and benchmarks remain largely limited to partial modality coverage, making it difficult to systematically evaluate full-modality representation learning. In this work, we take a step toward the full-modality setting. We introduce MMEB-V3, a comprehensive benchmark that evaluates embeddings across text, image, video, audio, as well as agent-centric scenarios. To enable more fine-grained diagnosis, we further construct OmniSET (Omni-modality Semantic Equivalence Tuples), where semantically equivalent instances are represented across modalities, allowing us to disentangle semantic similarity from modality effects. Through experiments on MMEB-V3, we conduct a systematic analysis of full-modality embeddings and identify three key findings: (1) models often fail to retrieve the intended target modality; (2) cross-modal retrieval is highly asymmetric and dominated by query-modality bias; and (3) instruction-induced shifts are either insufficient or misaligned with the target modality, and therefore do not reliably improve retrieval. These results indicate that current multimodal embeddings are not yet capable of reliably enforcing modality constraints specified by instructions, and consequently fail to exhibit consistent modality-aware retrieval behavior. We hope MMEB-V3 provides a useful benchmark for understanding and diagnosing these limitations, and for guiding future research on full-modality embeddings.

How to validate the effectiveness of review-oriented workflows has, however, remained a confusing and controversial topic in technology-assisted review (TAR) in the law. We examine the sources of this controversy, and propose a simple and practical evaluation approach for review-oriented workflows. Our Delayed Countdown method is easily incorporated into existing review-oriented workflows and software, is compatible with arbitrary stopping rules, and produces valid frequentist confidence intervals on effectiveness. ☆ iWAM: Efficient Action Prediction from World Models without Explicit Future Prediction

However, generating future scenes is expensive for real-time control. This motivates efficient proxies for future imagination, but how to train such proxies without sacrificing action-prediction quality remains unclear. An effective proxy need not generate a high-resolution frame; it only needs to provide enough information to distinguish between possible futures. This leads to the design principle behind iWAM: rather than denoising an entire future frame, can we condition the action policy on intermediate features from a single video-model evaluation? We show that the answer is yes. Exploiting the reversible dynamics of flow-matching models, we invert each training future into the corresponding latent noise vector. However, a single velocity evaluation at this latent does not necessarily yield informative features for action prediction. We therefore learn a bidirectional flow map that amortizes future-generation computation, enabling a single model evaluation to provide effective conditioning features. At inference, we sample a latent noise vector from the prior and condition the policy using just one video-backbone forward pass. Across simulated benchmarks and real robots, iWAM recovers the generalization benefits of WAMs while substantially reducing its inference cost.

Our results suggest that a standard temperature scaling applied to the draft distribution improves the acceptance length by up to approximately 10\% with almost no additional cost across different tasks. Throughput analysis further verifies that this improvement in serving efficiency. Analysis of more general calibration methods reveals further potential room for improvement.

Broadly speaking, reinforcement learning (RL) post-training converts compute into model capabilities by training on model-generated data. Typically, the rollouts are discarded after each update, and the knowledge acquired during RL resides in the model weights. In this work, we investigate how much of this knowledge is retained in the rollouts themselves. A natural first attempt is to replay the original RL algorithm on archived rather than freshly generated rollouts, but this leads to catastrophic collapse. We provide a simple explanation for this phenomenon, which in turn suggests a remedy: maximum likelihood on the archived rollouts. Surprisingly, starting from the same base model and replaying the rollouts in the order in which they were generated, without any distinction between correct and incorrect responses, is sufficient to recover the performance of online RL. In fact, a single maximum likelihood update per rollout batch closely tracks the entire learning curve of online RL. Furthermore, maximum likelihood on the rollouts of the last few RL steps often suffices to recover the final model's performance. This suggests that much of the compute invested in RL goes into discovering an improved sampling distribution rather than learning it from samples.

Efficient equidistant codes are therefore excluded: Hadamard codes ($M\ge 8$), which meet the Plotkin bound with $M-1$ columns, have no such pairs, and for the Sylvester type the reversal margin can be at least a constant 0.0182 independent of $M$. All theorems are machine-checked in Lean 4. On six real datasets with estimated probabilities, the product decoder is slightly more accurate when each column is calibrated, and the sum decoder is better when the calibration error differs across columns; in either case the decoders disagree only near ties.

Third, scalar UQ signals are weak at identifying which control has the larger clipped NDCG@10 difference, whereas source-specific signals, including Perturbation Rank Instability and simple listwise distances, provide stronger paired-control agreement, reflecting their sensitivity to the two controlled evidence sources. Here $S$ is the number of states, $H$ is the horizon, and $D:=\max_i\min\{H,1/ρ_i\}$, where $ρ_i$ is the TV radius of player~$i$. Two ingredients make this possible: a plug-in estimate of the robust backup whose mean error does not depend on the number of states, and a single batch of samples per round that serves as bandit feedback for all players at once. We propose NABLA, a noise-adaptive blockwise left-right preconditioning algorithm for mini-batch stochastic nonconvex optimization. Unlike conventional matrix-preconditioned methods that use fixed decay parameters, NABLA adjusts the second-moment averaging coefficient through a closed-loop feedback rule determined by the cumulative stochastic-gradient energy and its running average. The first-moment coefficient remains fixed, allowing the trajectory-dependent adaptation to act directly on the structured preconditioners. The resulting method is horizon-free, requires no prior knowledge of the noise level, and automatically adjusts the memory of its second-moment estimators to the observed optimization dynamics. Under standard lower boundedness, smoothness, unbiasedness, bounded-variance, and spectral-boundedness assumptions, we establish uniform stability and variation bounds for the time-varying block preconditioners and control their interaction with momentum estimation and parameter updates. These results yield the noise-adaptive stationarity guarantee $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(T^{-1/2}+σ^{1/2}T^{-1/4})$, which automatically reduces to the nearly deterministic $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(T^{-1/2})$ rate when the stochastic-gradient noise vanishes. NABLA therefore provides a principled approach to combining closed-loop trajectory feedback with memory-efficient structured matrix preconditioning.

A comprehensive evaluation on both synthetic and real datasets shows that OpenWoud maintains or increases accuracy (up to +12.89%), compared to a prior FPGA accelerator, while reducing the resource utilization by half. Competitive performance is observed compared to GPU (0.5 - 1.5x speed-up) and an FPGA baseline (0.2 - 0.5x), despite the latter being based on idealized simulation. With the growing scale of scientific simulation and infrastructure, part of the burden has shifted from producing scientific data to analyzing and storing it. Compression is a key step to expanding storage capacity, but requires dedicated techniques to enforce user-specified pointwise error bounds that ensure the validity of downstream scientific workflows. To further push the limits of compression, novel learned codecs have been developed, in particular for images and videos, but these methods often optimize for aggregated distortion and fail to meet error bound standards. Moreover, these methods often target fixed field dimensionality, failing to account for many scientific data use cases, or at the expense of large adaptation or retraining costs. In this work, we introduce the Learned Axial TEnsor Compression (LATEC) method, an error-bounded codec with a dimension-agnostic learned predictor based on a GNN architecture. LATEC is pretrained on synthetic 2-D and 4-D fields, and evaluated with and without domain fine-tuning on 13 scientific fields in 3-D to 5-D. Results show that LATEC is consistently competitive with SZ3, achieving an 18.1% average improvement and greater consistency across all domains than other compressors. These results demonstrate that a shared learned predictor can serve as a single error-bounded codec across tensor dimensionalities, competitive with specialized compressors, while retaining pointwise error guarantees.

For location-matched pairs, our model achieves a paired AUC of 0.706 for impairment detection on DIVERT, compared to 0.590 without reconstruction loss, improving over existing baselines. We plan to publicly release the code and data.

Mingyang Deng, He Li, Tianhong Li, Yilun Du, Kaiming He
Generative modeling can be formulated as learning a mapping f such that its pushforward distribution matches the data distribution. The pushforward behavior can be carried out iteratively at inference time, e.g., in diffusion/flow-based models. In this paper, we propose Drifting Models, a new generative modeling paradigm that evolves the pushforward distribution during training and naturally admits one-step inference. We introduce a drifting field that governs the sample movement and achieves equilibrium when the distributions match. This leads to a training objective that allows the neural network optimizer to evolve the distribution. In experiments, our one-step generator achieves state-of-the-art one-step results on ImageNet 256x256, with FID 1.54 in latent space and 1.61 in pixel space. We hope that our work opens up new opportunities for high-quality one-step generation.

♻ ☆ Convex-Concave Reinforcement Learning SC
Shripad V. Deshmukh, Yaswanth Chittepu, Dhawal Gupta, Philip Thomas, Scott Niekum
Policy learning drives many of the most consequential and heavily-invested applications of reinforcement learning today. Yet the core optimization problem it rests on (maximizing expected return) is notoriously non-convex, even under a direct policy parameterization, and the field has largely responded by avoiding it: optimizing convex surrogate approximations of the return under trust-region constraints (NPG, TRPO, PPO, AWR). We show that this seemingly unstructured problem is not actually structureless. In log-density-ratio coordinates $y := \log[π/π_n]$, the exact per-iteration objective, computable via per-decision importance sampling (PDIS), is a difference-of-convex-constrained difference-of-convex (DC-constrained DC) program. This structure lets us move beyond surrogate approximations: it recovers CPI, NPG, TRPO, and AWR as special cases along interpretable axes, and it opens a multi-step axis $k$ that couples consecutive decisions. We solve the per-iteration program with sequential convex programming (SCP), the standard solver for difference-of-convex problems, and establish inner-loop descent and limit-point stationarity for the theoretical algorithm, together with a conditional outer-loop performance bound. Empirically, multi-step Convex-Concave RL (CCRL) wins on diagnostic MDPs where credit must propagate across a horizon (its advantage growing with the dependency length), is competitive with a tuned PPO on classic control, and on a clinically motivated, stochastic, mid-horizon sepsis simulator converges markedly faster than tuned PPO to the same near-optimal survival, with an 11.3% higher area under the training curve. The code is publicly available at: https://github.com/UMass-SCALAR-Lab/Convex-Concave-RL

♻ ☆ Sparse Autoencoder Attribution Graphs Are Decided at the Margin
Karl Li
Interpretability research writes a language model's activation as a weighted sum of learned directions, called features. A sparse autoencoder (SAE) learns the features and gives each a coefficient, its weight in that sum. The SAE's encoder first gives every feature a score. A TopK SAE selects the k features with the largest positive scores and zeroes the rest. A feature's margin is how far its score must move before the selection changes. An intervention on one feature's coefficient changes the encoder scores of the SAE at the next layer. An attribution graph predicts that change from the scores' derivatives with respect to the coefficient, taken before the intervention. The graph keeps the original selection, so it misses every feature that enters or leaves. We propose the margin graph, which adds the predicted change to every score and selects again. When one feature is zeroed in a public pair of Pythia-70M SAEs, the median error of the predicted coefficient change, relative to the true change, falls from 0.739 for the attribution graph to 0.121 for the margin graph. Written back into the model, the margin graph's coefficients predict the change in the model's output on subject verb agreement less accurately than the attribution graph's. Selecting again better predicts which features change, but on the task and pair we tested, not the model's output.

♻ ☆ Announced Breaks Separate Conformal Reliability from Frequency Calibration NeurIPS 2026
Karl Li
A prediction interval should contain the outcome at a stated rate. Conformal prediction sets its width from past forecast errors. When the process behind a time series changes on an announced date, intervals set from errors before that break can stop covering. After Australia moved to five minute electricity settlement, a 90% interval fixed beforehand covered 51.5% of the next 400 days. One forecaster needs the next interval to cover, another a finished period's share of misses at 10%. We show that each need calls for its own restart at the date. We recompute the next interval from the $n$ errors since the break. If these errors are independent, its coverage comes within $O(n^{-1/2})$ of the stated rate, the best order attainable. For a finished period, we restart adaptive conformal inference (ACI). On bounded errors, if a floor under its width adds a bounded total, it brings the share of misses within $O(n^{-1})$ of target but promises nothing about the next interval. After a simulated mean shift of 5.0 noise standard deviations, recomputed intervals cover within 3.5 percentage points of 90% on average at the 50th forecast, a third closer than the 5.2 of the best of five baselines. Of nine announced breaks in power markets and at a central bank, restarting ACI gives a detectable gain only at the one large break.

♻ ★ RIBOSPAN: A Long-Context RNA Foundation Model for Versatile RNA Modeling
